title: Did Cao Cao Set the Red Cliffs Fire Himself? 800,000 Troops and Two Letters to Sun Quan
description:
Winter, 208 AD, on the Yangtze. Cao Cao's warships sat one after another, bow to stern, and then burned to ash. Afterwards he wrote to Sun Quan and said he had set that fire himself.

This episode follows the main text of the Records of the Three Kingdoms and the old books quoted in Pei Songzhi's annotations: the letter before the battle, "Now I have trained a navy of 800,000 and will hunt with you, General, in Wu"; the numbers Zhou Yu ran for Sun Quan (150,000-160,000 plus 70,000-80,000; he asks for 50,000 and gets 30,000, while his own biography has him ask for 30,000 from the start and Sun Quan's has him and Cheng Pu lead 10,000 each); the sickness already in Cao's camp before the fighting; Huang Gai's fake surrender letter and Cao Cao questioning the messenger in private; that day's southeast wind (Zhou Yu's biography says only "the wind was fierce"); ten fire ships that flew "like arrows"; and the single line in Zhuge Liang's biography, "Lord Cao was defeated at Red Cliffs and led his army back to Ye." Then Sun Quan's biography, "Lord Cao burned his remaining ships and withdrew; his men were starving and sick, and more than half died"; Liu Bei's biography, "burned his ships"; the muddy road at Huarong and the Shanyang Gong Zaiji's "Lord Cao's ships were burned by Liu Bei"; the second ship-burning at Baqiu and "Had Guo Jia lived, he would not have let me come to this"; "I am not ashamed to run"; and finally the letter Cao Cao wrote to Sun Quan after the battle, "At Red Cliffs we happened to meet with sickness; I burned my ships and withdrew, and so Zhou Yu won this fame for nothing", while the Annals of Emperor Wu say only "a setback" and "then a great plague". The chained ships, the self-inflicted beating, the borrowed east wind and Guan Yu letting Cao Cao go at Huarong are all plot from the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms; this episode sets them side by side with what the histories say.

Quotations follow the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu edition of the Records of the Three Kingdoms (with Pei Songzhi's annotations; two passages read differently in other editions: whether the ships were linked, and Cao Cao's remark on Liu Bei at Huarong, which this edition gives as "put out the fire" and others as "set the fire"; the narration uses wording that holds for both). The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below; sentences that begin "we think" are the channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten on 2026-10-25 under new guidelines)

chapters.open-you: The loser says he set the fire

rc001.text: You've surely seen this scene: Cao Cao's army, said to be 800,000 strong, wiped out by one fire.

rc003.text: Yet histories from 1,800 years ago can't even agree on who set the fire.

rc004.text: Winter, 208 AD, on the Yangtze: a man in his fifties stands on a ship, watching the far bank.

rc006.text: His warships sat one after another, bow to stern, and then burned to ash.

rc008.text: Oddly, he later wrote to his rival that he had set that fire himself.

rc009.text: But that's not the oddest. Before the battle, men in the northern camp fell ill one by one.

rc011.text: This file translates every Red Cliffs line in the Records, and Cao Cao's two letters.

rc012.text: So who really set the fire at Red Cliffs?

rc013.text: The fire was written down decades later, in the Records of the Three Kingdoms.

rc014.text: Its author, Chen Shou, once served Shu; after Shu fell, he wrote Wei, Shu and Wu into one book.

rc015.text: A later annotator added quotes from several old books. Do the text and notes always agree?

rc016.text: That year, say the records, Cao Cao went south. He took Jingzhou; Liu Biao's son Liu Cong yielded without a fight.

rc017.text: Liu Bei fled; Cao's 5,000 elite riders rode over 300 li in 24 hours and caught him at Changban.

rc018.text: Liu Bei abandoned his family and fled with a few dozen riders to Xiakou.

rc019.text: You're Sun Quan. Jingzhou next door just surrendered, Liu Bei is at your door. What do you do?

rc020.text: Liu Bei sent a young man to Wu for help.

rc021.text: His name was Zhuge Liang; he urged Sun Quan to ally.

rc022.text: Then, unexpectedly, Cao Cao wrote to Sun Quan too.

rc117.text: It opens with a boast: by the emperor's order I punish offenders; my banners turned south, and Liu Cong gave up.

rc023.text: Then he says he has a navy of 800,000, to "hunt with the General in Wu."

rc024.text: A joint hunt, that is. And who's the prey? No need to say.

rc025.text: The problem: at Wu's court, many urged Sun Quan to surrender.

rc026.text: Lu Su told Sun Quan privately: all of us can surrender, except you.

rc027.text: If we surrender, we still get posts; if you do, where can you go?

rc118.text: That line feels harsh to me, but it put Sun Quan first.

rc028.text: A Wu commander in his early thirties also opposed surrender. His name was Zhou Yu.

rc029.text: Sun Quan slashed off a desk corner: urge surrender again, and you're next.

rc030.text: But think: the corner's gone, yet the number in the letter is still there. Was that number true?

rc031.text: Zhou Yu's answer: don't be scared yet. That night he saw Sun Quan alone and did the math for him.

rc119.text: Everyone, he said, saw the number and panicked; nobody checked whether it was real.

rc032.text: Northern troops: just 150,000-160,000, tired from a long march.

rc033.text: Liu Biao's newly won men: at most 70,000-80,000, still wavering.

rc034.text: Add them up: nowhere near the letter's number. So how many men to stop them?

rc035.text: Zhou Yu said 50,000 crack troops would do it.

rc036.text: Short of 50,000 for now, Sun Quan gave him 30,000.

rc037.text: But that's from the Jiangbiao Zhuan in the notes; the Records' own text has Zhou Yu ask for 30,000 outright.

rc038.text: Sun Quan's chapter is even better: Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu each led 10,000 men. One book, three numbers. Which is right?

rc039.text: These numbers baffled me too, until it clicked: the book won't balance them for you; it records all it heard.

rc040.text: Remember the sick men from the start? The records say Cao's men were sick before the first clash.

rc041.text: At the first clash, Cao's forces fell back, mooring on the north bank.

rc042.text: North bank: a row of ships. South bank: a much smaller army. If this drags on, who breaks first?

rc043.text: Across the river, one look at those ships gave someone an idea.

rc044.text: It was Huang Gai, a veteran general under Zhou Yu.

rc045.text: He said: they're many, we're few; dragging it out hurts us.

rc046.text: Remember the ships lined bow to stern? Huang Gai said: they'll burn.

rc047.text: In the novel, a strategist tells Cao Cao to chain his ships together.

rc048.text: The records have no such strategist and no chains. So were the ships linked?

rc049.text: On whether they were linked, two editions of the Records differ; but "bow to stern" is in both.

rc050.text: Huang Gai packed dozens of warships with dry grass and firewood.

rc051.text: Doused in oil, then covered with cloth.

rc052.text: With flags flying, from afar they looked like ordinary warships. These ships were headed off to "surrender."

rc053.text: Each big ship towed a small fast boat for the getaway after the fire. But how would they reach Cao's camp?

rc054.text: But first, he wrote Cao Cao a letter. What did it say?

rc055.text: It said he owed Wu a great deal.

rc120.text: Yet six Jiangdong commanderies against a northern army "a million strong"? Clearly a losing fight.

rc121.text: So he'd bring his ships over and surrender.

rc056.text: Did you notice? The letter makes Cao's army bigger than Cao himself did.

rc122.text: The smartest touch in the letter.

rc057.text: How did Cao Cao take it?

rc058.text: Cao Cao had the messenger brought in and questioned him privately: I fear you're tricking me.

rc059.text: If it's true, Huang Gai's reward will top everyone's.

rc060.text: In the novel, Huang Gai takes a flogging to convince Cao: the "bitter flesh ruse."

rc061.text: This letter was fake. The flogging? The records don't mention it at all.

rc062.text: The records don't say how far Cao believed it. But before an answer, something else came.

rc063.text: It was wind. On the day of battle, a southeast wind blew, and it blew hard.

rc064.text: The wind is real; the records have it. The novel says Zhuge Liang borrowed it at the Seven Stars Altar.

rc065.text: In the records, nobody borrows it.

rc066.text: Look: the main text only says "the wind was fierce." No direction.

rc123.text: "Southeast" comes from the book the notes quote.

rc067.text: The wind was there, the ships too. But how to get near Cao's camp undetected?

rc068.text: Ten ships led the way; in midstream, they raised their sails.

rc069.text: Cao's sailors leaned out; men ashore came out to watch, pointing: "Huang Gai is surrendering!"

rc070.text: Just over 2 li out, every ship lit its fire at once.

rc071.text: The result? Fire and wind sent the ships flying like arrows.

rc072.text: Ships on the north bank burned, and the fire spread ashore. Soon smoke and flames hid half the sky.

rc074.text: Those who'd just pointed and gawked: can you picture their faces now?

rc073.text: Zhou Yu's elite followed, drums pounding. The north broke.

rc075.text: Honestly, the fire takes up far less text than I thought.

rc124.text: Cao's army fell back to Nanjun.

rc076.text: Oh, and the one you know best? What was Zhuge Liang up to?

rc077.text: His biography gives it one line: "Lord Cao lost at Red Cliffs and led his army to Ye."

rc078.text: It only says Sun Quan sent Zhou Yu's troops back with him to Liu Bei, not what he did that day.

rc079.text: But on how Cao Cao retreated, the records hide a line few people notice.

rc080.text: That line is in the Records' chapter on Wu, and it's just seven characters.

rc081.text: Cao burned his remaining ships and withdrew. Remember? He said he set that fire himself.

rc082.text: Eight more characters follow: his men starved and fell sick, and more than half died.

rc083.text: Most likely, we think: he could neither take the ships nor cede them.

rc084.text: Liu Bei's chapter notes it too: Cao crushed, his ships burned.

rc125.text: And chased to Nanjun, it says, the northern army fell sick again.

rc086.text: Then Huarong Road. The novel has Guan Yu wait there and let him go. And the records?

rc087.text: In the records, just a muddy road horses couldn't pass, under a strong wind.

rc088.text: He had frail soldiers lay straw so the cavalry could cross.

rc089.text: If you were Cao Cao on that road, you'd hardly laugh. But he did. Why?

rc090.text: Out of the mud, Cao suddenly laughed. His generals asked why.

rc091.text: He said: Liu Bei is my kind of man, just a bit slow with his plans.

rc092.text: Soon Liu Bei did light fires behind him, but Cao was already through.

rc093.text: The old book that records this muddy road opens with a harsher line: Cao Cao's ships were burned by Liu Bei.

rc126.text: That's strange. But the strangest line comes on his way back north.

rc094.text: Heading north, he reached Jiangling, left Cao Ren to hold it, and pressed on.

rc095.text: On that road, the records note another ship-burning. Why this time?

rc096.text: At a place called Baqiu, plague struck again; again he burned ships.

rc097.text: Watching the ships burn, he sighed: were Guo Jia alive, he'd never have let me come to this.

rc098.text: Guo Jia, his most trusted aide, died of illness the year before, at 38.

rc099.text: You've likely been there too: it all goes wrong, and you think, if only that person were still here.

rc100.text: On this battle, Cao Cao said a defiant line: "I am not ashamed to run." I fled, yes, but I feel no shame.

rc101.text: Not ashamed? Then why write later to explain the fire?

rc102.text: The letter survives in the Jiangbiao Zhuan, cited in the notes.

rc103.text: He wrote Sun Quan: at Red Cliffs we met with illness; I burned my ships and withdrew.

rc104.text: Zhou Yu won that fame for nothing.

rc105.text: The book that keeps it adds: Zhou Yu was so famous, Cao Cao and Liu Bei both wanted to smear him.

rc106.text: Remember the ten fire ships that hit Cao's camp? The letter says not a word.

rc107.text: And the sickness? The Records' chapter on Cao Cao gives Red Cliffs only "a setback" and "then a great plague."

rc108.text: Strangely, not one word about fire.

rc109.text: I find this fascinating: the chapter on Cao Cao and Cao Cao's own letter tell the same story. Sickness, not fire.

rc127.text: We think the two letters work the same way.

rc111.text: The one before the battle inflated his army; the one after shrank his defeat.

rc112.text: Like flunking a test and saying at home: I knew it, I just didn't want to.

rc113.text: So the Red Cliffs fire, by the Records' main text, was set by two men: Huang Gai to win, Cao Cao to leave.

rc115.text: As Sun Quan, holding that "hunt in Wu" letter: cut the desk corner, or surrender? Tell me below.

rc116.text: We only tell what's in the records. Subscribe to open files with us.
